title: Quantum simulation of real-world nonlinear dynamics via Koopman method
authors: Baoyang Zhang, Dong An, Zhaoyuan Meng, Yefei Yu, Xiaoxiao Xiao, Zhen Lu, Yue Yang
abstract: Nonlinear dynamics is ubiquitous in nature, ranging from chemical pattern formation to ocean circulation, yet its simulation on quantum computers is fundamentally limited by the unitary nature of quantum evolution. We propose the quantum Koopman method, a data-driven framework that embeds nonlinear dynamics into a learned linear representation and implements the resulting evolution using shallow quantum circuits. This method learns Koopman observables from trajectory data, projects the lifted dynamics onto a finite-dimensional subspace, and decomposes the corresponding non-unitary propagator into parallel spectral channels. We utilize the Koopman method on a superconducting processor to simulate three distinct nonlinear systems, comprising reaction-diffusion dynamics, fluid motion on a sphere, and satellite-derived observations of Gulf Stream currents, employing up to 32 parallel circuits of 10 qubits. These quantum simulations capture the dominant multiscale patterns and statistical signatures of the underlying dynamics, and reveal a transition from performance limited by hardware noise in weakly nonlinear systems to performance limited by finite-dimensional Koopman representations as nonlinear scale interactions increase. This transition identifies a practical boundary for quantum-amenable nonlinear dynamics, establishing a hardware-validated route for simulating moderately nonlinear dynamics on near-term quantum hardware.
summary: The paper introduces the Quantum Koopman Method (QKM) to overcome the limitation of unitary evolution when simulating nonlinear physical processes. By mapping these dynamics into a linear observable space, it implements the evolution using shallow, parallel quantum circuits on superconducting hardware. This approach successfully simulates complex fluid and reaction-diffusion systems while quantifying the theoretical limits imposed by finite representation size.
main_problem: The core challenge is simulating real-world nonlinear dynamics, which are fundamentally incompatible with the unitary evolution constraints of current quantum hardware.
main_result: The Quantum Koopman Method (QKM) successfully simulates complex systems like fluid dynamics and reaction-diffusion processes on superconducting processors, establishing a practical boundary for near-term quantum simulation.
method: It uses the QKM to map nonlinear dynamics into an infinite-dimensional linear observable space, projects this onto a finite subspace, and implements the resulting non-unitary evolution using shallow, parallel quantum circuits.
model_or_system: The method is tested on three benchmarks: 3D reaction-diffusion systems (Gray-Scott), shallow-water dynamics on a sphere, and real-world Gulf Stream current observations. The implementation uses superconducting transmon qubits.
key_observables: Relative $L_2$ error ($\ell$), enstrophy spectrum, vorticity field ($\omega$) evolution, and training/validation losses ($\ell_{train}, \ell_{val}$).
important_parameters: The simulation scales with grid resolution ($D$), number of qubits per circuit ($n = O(\log D)$), and the number of parallel spectral channels ($h=O(n)$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the dynamics can be accurately captured by a finite-dimensional Koopman subspace, and it relies on hybrid classical/quantum processing where an NN encoder prepares initial states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QKM schematic, the hardware-efficient quantum circuit structure (using $R_z$ layers), and comparisons of simulated dynamics against reference solutions for fluid motion and reaction-diffusion systems.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QKM framework by linearizing nonlinear evolution. It details the quantum implementation using spectral decomposition into parallel circuits. Validation is performed on three physical benchmarks, followed by ablation studies to quantify sources of error (spectral sampling vs. ansatz structure).
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, hardware-aware pathway for simulating complex, non-Hamiltonian dynamics that are central to many areas of AMO physics and open quantum systems research.
